community.headline: Volunteers wanted for Tesco winter food collection on 26 to 28 November
community.summary: Volunteers are sought for three-hour shifts at collection points in large Tesco stores, supporting Trussell food banks and the Felix charity network.
points: Shifts take about three hours
Last year's collection gave almost 1.5 million meals
body: Foodbanks and food charities are looking for volunteers to stand at collection points in large Tesco stores for the supermarket's Winter Food Collection, which runs from 26 to 28 November. Volunteering takes about three hours, and the charities say having people in store significantly increases how much food is given.

This is the 14th year of the collection, run with charity partners Trussell and Felix, and last year shoppers donated almost 1.5 million meals' worth of food. One in five Trussell food parcels comes from Tesco and its customers, and more than half of the charities in the Felix network, which spans over 8,000 local groups, report rising demand over the past year.

People can sign up through the Trussell or Felix websites to help at their nearest large Tesco. Trussell's co-chief executive Matthew van Duyvenbode said volunteers were urgently needed to play their part.

courts.headline: Eastwood dog owner to be sentenced in December after 15 German shepherds were rescued from his home
courts.summary: Terence Snooks was convicted of 15 animal welfare offences after a joint council and police raid, in what officers called one of the worst neglect cases they had seen in 30 years.
body: Terence Snooks, of Eastwood, was convicted at Basildon Magistrates’ Court on 1 September of 15 offences under section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act 2006, Southend-on-Sea City Council says. The case came after council and police officers removed 15 German shepherd dogs from a property in Eastwood in February 2025, following residents’ complaints about persistent barking and the state of the property.

The council says the dogs lacked proper food, fresh water, bedding, exercise and socialisation, and the house and garden were heavily contaminated with faeces and urine. Many of the animals had matted fur and overgrown claws, several were underweight, and three were so badly affected that they had to be put to sleep. Five went to a specialist breed rehabilitation centre and most of the rest have been rehomed.

ITV News reported the case on Wednesday. Snooks is due to be sentenced at Basildon Magistrates’ Court on 8 December. Councillor Irene Ferguson said the result showed the council would act on serious welfare concerns.

official.headline: Rochford leader urges ministers to lift block on Local Plan and allow more time to consult
official.summary: A Government holding direction in place since 2 October stops the council starting its final round of public consultation.
body: Rochford District Council has called on the Government to decide quickly on its Local Plan and lift the holding direction that has paused it since 2 October. The council says it cannot start the final public consultation while the direction stays in place, and is also asking for the submission deadline to be extended, which it believes could run to March.

Council leader Cllr Adi Malviya said the district needs an up-to-date plan to avoid speculative applications in the wrong places. The council says it sent the evidence ministers requested on 7 October, and that before the direction it was on track to submit by the 31 December deadline.

If the direction is lifted without an extension, the council says consultation would probably run over Christmas and close on the day the plan must be submitted, leaving councillors no time to consider responses. Separately, the public inquiry into the Mount Bovers appeal on land west of Main Road, Hawkwell, resumes on 8 December.

body: Tendring District Council has granted Clacton Town Football Club Ltd a temporary licence to use the Rush Green Bowl on Rush Green Road, Clacton, for the rest of the 2026/27 season. The council says the licence formalises the club’s current occupation of the council-owned ground, with safeguards for the site, and keeps it open for football and community use.

The council says it has been working to resolve longstanding issues around the ground’s occupation. Councillor Peter Kotz, cabinet member for assets, said the licence keeps football going at the site and welcomed improvements the club has made to the ground.
Next, the council plans an open and fair tender for a longer-term lease. It says whoever wins the lease may be able to apply for Football Association funding.

body: Southend-on-Sea City Council has opened the final round of public consultation on its draft Local Plan, the document that will guide where new homes, employment land, infrastructure and community facilities may go across the city. It runs from Friday 6 November until Monday 21 December 2026.

The council said central government formally directed it on 23 October to publish the draft for consultation by 6 November, and the cabinet agreed unanimously on 5 November to do so. Comments at this stage must address whether the plan is legally compliant and sound under national planning policy. Cllr Kevin Robinson, cabinet member for planning, property and governance, urged residents to read the draft and respond.

Documents and the response form are on the council's Local Plan website, with paper copies at Southend libraries and the Civic Centre reception. Full council is due to consider the final plan in early 2027, when it will be submitted for independent examination by a planning inspector.

Around 40 former Idverde employees moved across, and council and Amphora staff marked the change with volunteering days at Castle Park on 2 and 3 November, clearing leaves and planting hundreds of spring bulbs. The service covers almost 13,000 assets over more than 870 hectares. Cllr Martin Goss, portfolio holder for waste, neighbourhoods and leisure, welcomed the new colleagues into the council family.
The council says the arrangement gives it more flexibility to respond to local priorities and to find new ways of improving parks and green spaces, while keeping investment in the local area.

body: Essex Police is appealing for witnesses after men claiming to be police officers approached people in Tilbury between 4am and 4.45am on Saturday 7 November. Police say the men were not in uniform and showed no identification, and nobody was hurt.

In one incident near the Tesco Express on Calcutta Road, two men got out of a white car and took a man's wallet and keys, police said. Officers say a taxi driver was also targeted on St Chads Road and another man was approached in the area. Police described three men, one in a high-visibility jacket and two in dark tracksuits, using a large white SUV-style car.

Grays CID is asking anyone who saw anything, or who was driving in the area with a dash cam, to come forward. Police say genuine officers will show their warrant card when asked and understand if people want to check their identity.

stories.headline: Roper twins back at the University of Essex after double Commonwealth Games bronze for Wales

body: Gymnasts Emily and Abigail Roper have returned to the University of Essex, where they study Sports and Exercise Science at the Colchester campus, after making Commonwealth Games history for Wales, the university reports. The 21-year-old twins were back on campus in their Essex Blades kit, holding up their Team Wales shirts from Glasgow 2026.

Abigail won bronze on vault with a score of 13.433, Wales' first Commonwealth Games vault medal since 1994. Emily, who had just missed out on the vault podium in fourth, took bronze on the uneven bars less than an hour later.

The sisters joined Essex on a sports scholarship in autumn 2025 with Glasgow as their goal. They train at Pipers Vale Gymnastics Club in Ipswich and also compete for the Essex Blades in student competitions, where Emily won gold and Abigail bronze at the BUCS championships in February.

Its hospital systems are working normally, patients should carry on attending unless they are contacted, and its phone lines are open as usual.

Microsoft says traffic is gradually being restored and that mailbox access and the processing of delayed email are improving, although it warns that some users may still see intermittent problems or late messages. To stop mail stuck in the backlog from being lost, it has extended the time it holds undelivered email to 48 hours.

Hospitals, GP surgeries and police forces across the UK were caught up in the outage, PA reports, and NHS Essex has apologised for slow email replies. The National Pharmacy Association warned that the disruption affects pharmacies' ability to contact GP practices and some patients, which could hold up prescriptions.

stories.summary: The university, which has campuses in Chelmsford plus Cambridge and Peterborough, spends about £150m a year on its workforce, the BBC reports.
body: Staff were told of the plan at a meeting earlier this week, the BBC has learned. ARU has opened a voluntary severance scheme as it tries to take millions of pounds out of its pay bill.

The university said that, like others in England, it was under significant financial pressure and had to manage its spending carefully to protect its long-term future. Acting now, a spokesman said, would keep "high-quality education and research across all our campuses" going.

Dr John Hogan, president of the University and College Union branch at ARU and a senior lecturer at the Cambridge campus, said he believed the cause was difficulty recruiting overseas students since immigration rules changed. The union has not yet been given details of the university's finances, he added. One staff member, speaking anonymously, told the BBC they did not blame financial mismanagement but the struggle to attract international students.

Most international students have been barred from bringing family members to the UK since January 2024, and Home Office figures published this week show student visa applications fell by a fifth in the year to October. ARU's 2024-25 annual report put its staffing costs at almost £159m, and it employed 1,410 academic staff that year, according to the Higher Education Statistics Agency.

ARU is the latest university in the region to cut costs. The University of Essex closed its Southend campus in August, with 400 jobs going across the institution, and the universities of East Anglia and Northampton have also cut jobs in recent years.

stories.headline: Inquest opens into death of Chelmsford boy, 2, who fell from Cyprus hotel window
stories.summary: Jaxon Foster died from multiple severe injuries on the first day of a family holiday in July, Essex Coroner's Court has heard.
body: Jaxon fell around 12 metres (nearly 40ft) from a fourth-floor window at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas, near Paphos, on 12 July. The inquest, opened and adjourned on Friday, heard that his provisional cause of death was severe head injuries and multiple injuries to his body and vital organs. He was confirmed dead in hospital later that day.
Lincoln Brookes, Essex's senior coroner, called it a "particularly tragic" case and offered his condolences to the family.

The family had landed in Cyprus only hours earlier and spent the afternoon by the pool. At around 6pm, Jaxon, his father and his grandfather were heading to a lift to go to dinner when the boy spotted a waterpark outside. His father, Joshua Foster, 37, an auditor, lifted him onto a windowsill so he could see the view, not realising that part of the window was open, and Jaxon fell before he could react.

In October, a court in Paphos fined Mr Foster €3,000 (about £2,500) after he admitted causing his son's death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. The judge found the window did not appear to carry markings that would have shown one section was open, said there was no evidence he had deliberately put Jaxon at risk, and said no sentence could match the family's loss. His lawyer described what happened as a momentary error with fatal consequences.
In an earlier statement, the family said Jaxon was deeply loved and would be missed forever.

stories.summary: A misconduct hearing chaired by Essex Police Chief Constable Rachel Nolan found Nicholas Davies did not stop, turn round or report the rider he had seen in Chelmsford.
body: Davies was on duty on the evening of 25 March 2026, driving towards the Army & Navy roundabout in Chelmsford, when his body-worn camera recorded a cyclist riding in the dark towards oncoming traffic, the Bishop's Stortford Independent reports. Essex Police's notice of the hearing placed the rider on the A1114 Essex Yeomanry Way and said Davies had shortly before been sent to another incident. Members of the public later reported the cyclist.

At about 12.20am on Thursday 26 March, the cyclist was involved in a collision with two vehicles on the northbound A130 at the Rettendon Turnpike and died at the scene. The road was shut between Howe Green and Rettendon for several hours, and police appealed at the time for sightings of a cyclist in black clothing on a white mountain bike between the A1114 and the A130. The cyclist has not been named in reports.

In the days that followed, Davies looked up reports of the crash on police systems and watched his own camera footage. The hearing notice said he had no lawful policing purpose for checking those records and did not disclose that he had already seen the cyclist on the road. Nolan found every allegation proven at the accelerated hearing on Thursday 12 November, saying his actions fell "well below the standard expected" of Essex Police officers.

stories.headline: Air ambulance downwash seriously injured woman filming its take-off near Southend Airport, report finds
stories.summary: Accident investigators say the Essex & Herts Air Ambulance crew could not see the woman behind a hedge in Southend and flew on unaware she had been hurt.
body: The woman had stepped out of her house to record the helicopter leaving a private field next to Southend Airport railway station at 6.08pm on Saturday 28 February 2026, and was standing by a parked car about 30 metres away when the blast of air from its rotors knocked her down. A relative helped her and she was taken to hospital, according to an Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) report published on 12 November.

The AW169 had landed in the field at about 5.46pm so its two paramedics could reach a patient in the homes east of the airport, and with sunset close the two pilots planned to fly night training at the airport before coming back for them. The commander asked bystanders with children by a fence to cross the road, and the crew waited for a train to leave the station before lifting off. The helicopter climbed almost vertically to 200ft but drifted east towards the road, and investigators say the hedge, the house and the parked car may have funnelled and strengthened the downwash.

The crew flew back to North Weald Airfield without knowing anyone had been injured, and the operator only learned of it when a relative got in touch four days later. The commander told investigators the hedge hid the houses from his view and that he would have warned the woman had he seen her. On 29 May 2026 the operator issued an instruction to all its pilots reminding them that downwash is a hazard on take-off as well as on landing.

stories.headline: Essex police commissioner warns of cuts to the force if its share of council tax is not raised
stories.summary: Roger Hirst, the Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner for Essex, says the police service across the county would shrink without a bigger precept in 2027/28.
body: Mr Hirst told Hits Radio the government had advised him to increase the policing part of council tax, and that refusing would cost Essex £8.5m in central grant. Planned improvements to Essex County Fire and Rescue Service would also be off the table, he said, but he will not decide until residents have had their say because of the cost-of-living crisis.

His precept survey, which takes about four minutes online, has been extended by two weeks after more than 750 responses. He said recorded crime in Essex is 15% below its September 2019 peak and knife crime has fallen 24% since 2019, though overall crime rose 2% in the 12 months to August 2026. Fire crews attended 6,580 incidents between 25 May and 23 August, 36% above the 2021 to 2025 average.

The Home Office said police funding nationally is at a record £18.5bn, with an extra £396m in grant this year, and that council tax is a local decision for commissioners. Mr Hirst, who says Essex gets an unfair share of national policing money, will use the survey results to shape his budget and precept proposals.
points: Survey closes on Wednesday 25 November
Hits Radio and Your Harlow both carried his appeal
Home Office says it is giving forces an extra £396m this year

body: Blackhawk, which arranges cover for builders and construction firms from its Westcliff-on-Sea base, has joined the London-based Clear Group, the trade title Insurance Business reported on 13 November. Managing director Mark Kemp said the move would let the firm keep the personal service and industry knowledge its clients value. Clear says it will invest in the business and open up the wider group's markets to its customers.

body: Braintree District Council said on Thursday 12 November that the Home Office had submitted its application for the Wethersfield asylum centre through the Urgent Crown Development process, which lets the Government seek permission directly rather than through the local planning authority. The current permission for the site runs out in April 2027.

Council leader Tom Cunningham called the news "incredibly disappointing" and said it would be the third time the Government had tried to get round the council's planning powers. The council says it will take legal advice on the basis for any decision to extend the site this way; it fought the use of the airbase in the courts between March 2023 and May 2024. Essex County Council leader Peter Harris told BBC News earlier in the week that Wethersfield was the wrong facility in the wrong location, while the Home Office said it was closing asylum hotels and moving people to former military sites.

The site has housed asylum seekers since July 2023. Braintree District Council says it wants it closed as soon as possible, and will keep up its weekly contact with the Home Office and the multi-agency forum it co-chairs with Essex County Council, Essex Police and health partners while the centre stays open.
stories.headline: Home Office bypasses Braintree council in bid to keep Wethersfield asylum centre open past April 2027
points: Urgent Crown Development lets the Government seek permission directly

stories.headline: No direct summer flight from Stansted to Florence once British Airways leaves the airport
stories.summary: British Airways CityFlyer is pulling out of the Uttlesford airport after the 2026/27 ski season, but Ryanair will keep flying to Bergerac, Nice, Olbia and Palma.
body: The last scheduled British Airways flights from Stansted leave on Sunday 11 April 2027, Chelmsford City Hub reports. The airline's summer timetable for next year drops all five of its warm-weather routes from the airport: Bergerac, Nice, Florence, Olbia in Sardinia and Palma de Mallorca.

Nice had been flown daily, Palma three times a day and Olbia twice a week, according to Simple Flying. Most of that demand will not be stranded: Ryanair plans to keep flying from Stansted to Bergerac, Nice, Olbia and Palma next summer, and Jet2 and TUI serve some of the same airports.

British Airways said it regularly reviews its network against demand and will use the aircraft elsewhere. It has not said whether the routes were losing money. CityFlyer first flew from Stansted in 2016, stopped during the Covid-19 pandemic and came back in 2024; its main base remains London City Airport.

Geneva and Chambéry ski flights run until then

stories.headline: Southend publishes three-year SEND plan after inspectors call for improvements
stories.summary: Better education, health and care plans and quicker access to neurodevelopmental support are among the aims of the Southend SEND Partnership's new action plan.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council published the Southend SEND Strategic Action Plan 2026 to 2029 on Thursday 12 November, setting out how schools, health services and the council will improve support for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities. It answers an Ofsted and Care Quality Commission inspection of the Southend-on-Sea Local Area Partnership earlier in 2026.

Inspectors praised committed staff across education, health and care and strong joint working, but found areas to improve. The plan targets five: preparing young people for adulthood, the quality of Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and their annual reviews, more consistent inclusion across schools, access to neurodevelopmental and mental health support, and how the partnership measures the impact of its work.

The partnership describes the plan as a live document that will keep changing. Views gathered through Your Say Southend for a refresh of the SEND Strategy 2027 to 2029 will be reviewed and added where needed, and the full plan is on the Livewell Southend website.
points: Inspection was carried out by Ofsted and the CQC earlier in 2026

body: Tesco opened its new Express store on Defoe Parade, Chadwell St Mary, on Thursday 12 November, Your Thurrock reports. Store manager Adnan Mohamed, who has worked for Tesco for 20 years, said it was his second store opening this year.
The shop will pass surplus food to local charities at the end of each day through Tesco's Community Food Connection scheme.

stories.summary: Officers in Thurrock teamed up with the Motor Insurers' Bureau for a one-day push against drivers with no cover.
body: The 36 cars were seized in Thurrock on Tuesday 10 November, along with four e-scooters and an e-bike, Your Thurrock reports. The day was part of Operation Drive Insured, which runs from 9 to 15 November.

One person was arrested on suspicion of drug-driving and immigration offences, a stolen vehicle was recovered and 50 traffic offence reports were issued, for offences from no MOT to using a phone at the wheel.
points: One vehicle was ordered off the road because of its poor condition
Operation Drive Insured runs until 15 November

stories.headline: Suspected drug-drivers in Essex barred from driving for up to six weeks while police investigate
stories.summary: Essex Police says it is one of the first forces in the country to use bail conditions this way, as drug-driving arrests across the county keep rising.
body: Essex Police is using bail conditions to stop people suspected of drug-driving from driving while its inquiries continue, the BBC reported on Thursday 12 November 2026. Adam Pipe, head of the force's roads policing unit, said the aim was to speed up justice, because court backlogs and delays in testing blood samples can leave suspects driving for months before any disqualification.

Your Harlow reports that the policy, introduced in July, lets a custody sergeant attach a condition not to drive to pre-charge bail when a suspect cannot be charged straight away, for example while blood or urine results are still awaited. The suspect can make representations before the custody sergeant decides.

Essex Police says the condition may be used after collisions causing serious injury, after dangerous driving following a police pursuit, or when a driver is already awaiting prosecution for another drink or drug driving offence. Mr Pipe described it as an interim driving restriction before a case reaches court.
points: Almost 2,000 drug-driving arrests in the first 10 months of 2026, against 886 for drink-driving

stories.headline: Burnham-on-Crouch signs friendship pact with Carpathian town of Yaremche
stories.summary: Burnham-on-Crouch Town Council has become the first in Essex to twin with a Ukrainian community, linking the River Crouch town with Yaremche in the Ivano-Frankivsk region.
body: Burnham-on-Crouch Town Council held a twinning ceremony with Yaremche, a town on the River Prut in Ukraine's Carpathian Mountains, at 10am on Thursday 12 November 2026, the Lviv Herald reports. The event in the council chambers was set to include a memorandum of friendship and cooperation and an exchange of civic gifts.
The link was built by Councillor Stephen Stratton through talks with Yaremche's mayor, Andriy Myronyak. Burnham has been twinned with L'Aiguillon-sur-Mer in France since 1980.
points: Mayor Councillor Douglas Bown opened the ceremony
Yaremche relied on tourism before Russia's full-scale invasion and has housed displaced people

stories.summary: Thurrock Council will consider objections to selling the Tilbury plots if they are lodged by 5pm on Friday 27 November 2026.
body: The Tilbury sites are a grass area on Russell Road, a small plot on Monarch Close, nine acres north of Parker Avenue and a strip between Dock Road and the railway towards East Tilbury, Thurrock Nub News reports. stories.headline: Colchester's Shrub End sports centre could get two new floodlit 3G pitches under £2m-plus plan
stories.summary: Colchester City Council and Colchester United Community Foundation have applied for planning permission to expand the Shrub End Community and Sports Centre, with the Football Foundation paying most of the cost.
body: The Shrub End site in Colchester already draws almost 2,000 people a week, and a supporting report finds the city is short of 5.5 full-size football pitches. The application, announced by Colchester City Council on Thursday 12 November, also covers an upgraded existing 3G pitch, extra spectator toilets, a pitch-side kitchen and a bigger car park.

The Football Foundation, backed by the Premier League, The FA and the Government, would put in more than £2 million, alongside money from Colchester United Community Foundation and section 106 contributions the council has set aside for sport. Corin Haines, chief executive of the foundation, which has run the centre with the council since 2006, said years of planning and consultation had led to this point.

The council says the scheme will be decided through its normal planning process, and residents can comment on the application through its planning portal during consultation. Essex County FA, the lead body for grassroots football in the county, supports the plans, which the partners say would open up more year-round sport for women and girls, disabled people and older residents.
points: Almost 2,000 people use the site each week

stories.headline: Billericay switches on its Christmas lights on 26 November, with a 150-stall market to follow
stories.summary: Billericay's town centre business group is staging a free late-night shopping evening on the High Street, and a Rotary club is running a free-entry market in December.
body: Billericay Town Council's chairman and Father Christmas will switch on the High Street lights at 5.30pm on Thursday 26 November, followed by a carol singalong, Phoenix FM reports. Your Billericay, the town's Business Improvement District, runs the evening from 4pm to 8pm with fairground rides and the Billericay Lions sleigh, and the top of the High Street will be closed to traffic.
The Rotary Club of Billericay Mayflower's market follows on Sunday 6 December, from 11am to 5pm, with a stage, Santa's parade and a free grotto.
points: Free parking for the market at Billericay Station, Radford Way, Lake Meadows and Sun Corner
The Rotary club says it has raised more than £500,000 in its first 13 years

stories.headline: Gibberd Garden creative space and Parndon Mill festival share in Harlow's £75,000 arts pot
stories.summary: Harlow's Cultural Enabler Grant Scheme, backed by Arts Council England, is funding young writers and SEND acting groups as well as new creative spaces in the town.
body: A new creative space at the Gibberd Garden and a community festival at Parndon Mill are among the projects funded by Harlow Council's £75,000 cultural grants round, announced on Thursday 12 November.

Harlow Council Leader Councillor Dan Swords said the town had long had cultural talent and needed "a bigger stage". Councillor Danielle Brown, cabinet member for culture and community, said the money would help more people find and join in with the town's creative life. The council has not published how many groups were funded or how much each received.

The grants run alongside building work on an Arts and Cultural Quarter in front of Harlow Playhouse, part of the Building Harlow's Future programme. Plans there include a live performance venue, a new home for the Gibberd Gallery, a music school, recording studios and an outdoor amphitheatre; no completion date has been given.
points: Money comes from Harlow Council and Arts Council England
Young writers and SEND acting groups also supported
No completion date yet for the Playhouse cultural quarter

stories.summary: Essex Police's Operation Limit stopped drivers across the Chelmsford area and turned up crimes that had nothing to do with driving.
body: Fourteen of the people arrested during the operation on Saturday 7 November 2026 were suspected of drink or drug driving, Chelmsford City Hub reports, citing Essex Police. Officers also detected 137 speeding offences and seized six vehicles.

One disqualified, uninsured driver with a foreign licence was found with cigarettes suspected to be counterfeit, a case now being taken forward with Trading Standards. Essex Police says enforcement will step up before its Christmas drink and drug-driving campaign.

stories.summary: Building work continues on the OnSide Youth Zone in Tilbury, which will offer climbing, music production, fitness and affordable hot meals for Thurrock's young people.
body: Construction is continuing on the OnSide Youth Zone in Tilbury, which is due to open in 2027, Thurrock Nub News reported on Thursday 12 November 2026. Bethanie Cundy, chief executive of OnSide Youth Zone Thames Gateway, said the charity's Generation Isolation findings showed why the centre matters for Thurrock.
OnSide says only 11% of young people in the South East attend youth clubs, and is asking local businesses to back the project.

stories.summary: Thurrock dance charity CoDa has brought its Beyond the Darkness installation to Tilbury Library and Hub until Monday 7 December.
body: CoDa Dance Company, a Thurrock dance charity, has opened its award-winning interactive installation Beyond the Darkness at Tilbury Library and Hub, Thurrock Nub News reported on Thursday 12 November 2026. It pairs a sensor screen that gets visitors moving with short dance films about life with multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's and acquired brain injury, made with neuro-disabled consultants.
Artistic director Nikki Watson founded the charity in 2013. The work was shown earlier at the Thameside in Grays.

stories.headline: Six-vehicle M25 crash between the M11 and Waltham Abbey brings hour-long delays to morning rush
stories.summary: Two of the four anticlockwise lanes near Waltham Abbey had reopened after the pile-up, with Essex Police saying nobody was reported hurt.
body: Six vehicles crashed on the anticlockwise M25 between junction 27 (M11) and junction 26 (Waltham Abbey) at about 6.30am on Thursday 12 November, the BBC reports.
Traffic was held at first. National Highways said drivers faced delays of about an hour, and Essex Police said there were no reported injuries.

Traffic was held before lanes began to reopen

stories.headline: Agency nurse told Colchester care home colleague he would 'kill' his whole family, panel finds
stories.summary: A Nursing and Midwifery Council panel found Rupesh Patel, 40, was drunk on a night shift at The Oaks care home in Colchester when he threatened a colleague, and he is set to be struck off.
body: The incident happened overnight on 12 to 13 November 2022, BBC News reports. As well as threatening the colleague's family, the panel found, Patel said he would 'hunt' the colleague down.

The panel also found he was under the influence at work on several occasions in late 2022, and the BBC says he was convicted of drink-driving in 2023. Patel denied drinking at work and denied using threatening language.
points: He worked across Suffolk and Essex, including at homes in Sudbury and near Ipswich
The striking-off order takes effect unless he appeals within 28 days

stories.headline: Hanningfield among England's most depleted reservoirs as Essex hosepipe ban enters fourth month
stories.summary: Hanningfield and Abberton, which supply much of mid and south Essex, held 37% of their capacity on 10 November, below average for the time of year, Essex & Suffolk Water says.
body: In June, the company's total supply stood at 83%, the BBC reports. Katie Davies, Essex & Suffolk Water's head of water service planning, told the BBC the November level was "below where we'd expect to be at this time of year".
Essex & Suffolk Water brought in a Temporary Use Ban, or hosepipe ban, at 00:01 on Monday 3 August 2026 after a long hot and dry spell. It says the ban remains in force across its supply area.

The BBC reports that the Environment Agency still lists the East of England as in drought and names Hanningfield among eight reservoirs or reservoir groups in England with exceptionally low levels. The company says its advice to conserve water will stay in place until a considerable amount of rain has fallen.
points: Total supply stood at 83% in June, the BBC reports
Hosepipe ban in force since 00:01 on Monday 3 August 2026
Environment Agency still lists the East of England as in drought

stories.headline: Senior doctors' walkout that threatened Harlow hospital appointments is paused for pay talks
stories.summary: Consultants at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow and across England will no longer strike later this month after the British Medical Association paused action to negotiate with the government.
body: Patients at Princess Alexandra Hospital had been warned to expect disruption to appointments and planned operations from 6.59am on Wednesday 25 November, when consultants were due to walk out for two days and provide emergency cover only. The hospital had asked people to keep their appointments unless contacted, Your Harlow reported.

The BMA's consultants committee, led by co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, called off the action on 11 November to open talks with the government, NewsWire Explorer reports. Consultants received a 3.5% rise this year; the union wants the standard week cut from 40 to 35 hours, better pay for out-of-hours work and changes to pensions.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper called it welcome news for patients and the wider NHS. Formal negotiations could begin in the week of 12 November, though ministers say a bigger pay rise this year is not on offer. In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who voted backed action, on a turnout of just over half.
points: The action would have run from 6.59am on Wednesday 25 November to 6.59am on Friday 27 November
Consultants want the standard week cut from 40 to 35 hours

stories.headline: Purfleet grandmother says rats are still keeping her family out of their Chieftain Drive council home
stories.summary: A Thurrock Council tenant in Purfleet says her family cannot move back in, while a ward councillor has asked the council for an action plan with timescales.
body: Lisa Clark, a Thurrock Council tenant on Chieftain Drive in Purfleet, told Thurrock Nub News in a report published on Wednesday 11 November 2026 that her family still cannot live in their home because of a rat infestation, after rats were found on her four-year-old granddaughter's bed. She says neighbours can hear rats in their walls.

Labour ward councillor Aaron Green says there has been little meaningful progress and the bin sheds are likely to be contributing; he has asked for a plan covering pest control, bin areas, support for the family and compensation.
points: Cabinet member Robert Willoughby has already apologised to the family
Reform ward councillor Michelle Heal says she is confident the council will resolve it

stories.headline: Chelmsford MP says Broomfield Hospital trust's recovery plan is moving too slowly
stories.summary: Marie Goldman wants clearer reporting on how the intensive NHS programme for Mid and South Essex will be judged, while the trust says waiting lists are already falling.
body: Liberal Democrat MP for Chelmsford Marie Goldman has criticised the pace of the intensive recovery programme for Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Broomfield Hospital, Chelmsford City Hub reported on Wednesday 11 November 2026. The programme began in September 2026, about six months after it was announced in March.
The trust says the programme is already shortening waiting lists and speeding up discharges, and the Department of Health and Social Care says early signs of progress are emerging.
points: 50.4% of the trust's planned-care patients were within 18 weeks, against a national median of 65.2%

stories.summary: Essex Police say the car is reported to have gone through red lights at the Old House Croft crossing near Burnt Mill School in Harlow on Halloween evening and then left the scene.
body: Two pedestrians were struck at the crossing beside Old House Croft, near First Avenue in Harlow, at about 6.45pm on Saturday 31 October, and one suffered a potentially serious leg injury, Essex Police said.
Police say the small car was heading from the Aldi area towards the town centre. Anyone with information or footage should quote incident 1197 of 31 October.

stories.headline: Southend Hospital becomes first in Essex to win Sophie's Legacy award for looking after children's families
stories.summary: Southend Hospital's Neptune children's ward now provides meals for parents staying with their child and play specialists seven days a week.
body: Only five other hospitals in the country hold the accreditation, Chelmsford City Hub reports. Sophie's Legacy was set up by Charlotte Fairall in memory of her daughter Sophie, who died of a rare childhood cancer, and hospitals must meet at least three of its five aims for families. The ward worked with caterer Medirest on the changes, which include a children's menu. Amy Taylor, associate director of nursing for paediatrics, said caring for a child also means caring for their family.

stories.headline: Brentwood centre for rape and sexual assault survivors reopens after refit with new aftercare rooms
stories.summary: The Essex Sexual Assault Referral Centre, paid for by the county's police commissioner with Essex Police, stays in the county so survivors need not travel elsewhere.
body: The Essex Sexual Assault Referral Centre in Brentwood has reopened after a refurbishment that brought upgraded medical equipment, secure storage for forensic evidence, tighter security and new rooms for aftercare following an examination, Your Thurrock reports.

Medical, practical and emotional help is offered to adults and children whether or not they go to the police. Commissioner Roger Hirst welcomed the reopening, and the Victims Commissioning Fund will help with future running costs.
points: Changes include better access for people with sight, hearing or mobility needs

stories.headline: Thurrock cabinet asked to scrap modular council homes plan and write off almost £400,000
stories.summary: Officers say the Thurrock scheme, which included homes for Afghan families who supported British forces, no longer offers value for money.
body: The plan was for 14 modular social homes in Thurrock, backed by a £1.8m government grant, with the ten not set aside for Afghan families going to households in temporary accommodation. Officers point to cost inflation, delivery risks and government timescales, Thurrock Nub News reports.
points: Cabinet decides on Wednesday 18 November 2026

stories.headline: Festoon lights back on Southend Pier for the first time in over 20 years, with switch-on set for Saturday
stories.summary: More than a mile of lights will run the length of the pier, launching an evening of festive events across the city on 14 November.
body: Southend Pier's festoon lighting is returning for the first time in more than two decades, Southend-on-Sea City Council has announced. More than a mile of the lights will stretch along the world's longest pleasure pier, and new colourful neon lighting and light-up benches have been added at the On the Decks area at the Pier Head.

The official pier switch-on is at 5pm on Saturday 14 November, with music, food and drinks at the Royal Pavilion afterwards. Council leader Daniel Cowan said the council had promised to bring the lights back and had done so, while cabinet member Matt Dent called it a special occasion for the city.

The same evening the main city centre Christmas lights are switched on at Victoria Circus at 6pm, followed by the season's last seafront fireworks at 7.30pm. Southend City BID's Christmas in the City runs on the High Street during the day, with an artisan market, live music and family activities.
points: Pier open 10.15am to 8pm on the day
Walking admission £3.10 for adults, £2.10 for children and concessions

stories.headline: Thurrock bus journeys capped at £2 from Monday until New Year's Eve
stories.summary: Thurrock Council's festive fare cap means no single bus trip starting in the borough will cost more than £2, weeks before the national cap falls to the same level.
body: The Festive Fare Cap starts on Monday 16 November 2026 and runs until 31 December, covering any single bus journey that begins in Thurrock, Your Thurrock reported on 11 November. The council says the Department for Transport pays for it, so it costs the authority nothing extra.
From 1 January 2027 the national cap drops from £3 to £2 across England outside London. Thurrock deputy leader Alan Benson said cheaper fares would help residents reach jobs, training and healthcare.
points: The scheme is funded by the Department for Transport
The national cap is backed by an extra £400 million

body: Three people were arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm with intent after a man was stabbed in East Walk, Basildon town centre, at about 6.20pm on Tuesday 10 November, Greatest Hits Radio Essex reports.
Medics treated the man before he was taken to hospital. The investigation is continuing and police are asking anyone with information or footage to come forward.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon council agrees to buy two plots at Langford to protect wildlife habitat from inappropriate use
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council will try to buy two parcels of land at Langford, near Maldon, sold at auction in 2025, and can pay up to 10% above an independent valuation to secure the deal.
body: Maldon District Council agreed on Thursday 22 October 2026 to purchase two parcels of land at Langford, near Maldon, in order to protect the existing natural habitat and reduce the risk of inappropriate future use. The decision was taken at a meeting of the full council, which had earlier deferred the matter until an independent valuation was completed.

The minutes say the plots were sold at auction in 2025 and the current owner has indicated a willingness to discuss a sale. Councillors were told the land has no vehicular access and limited potential for other development but is suitable for environmental use, that Essex Wildlife Trust has expressed interest in exploring a lease, and that the housebuilder Vistry has offered to improve the footpath across one of the plots. The report proposed discretion to pay up to 5% above the valuation, but the Leader of the Council moved an amendment raising this to 10%, which was agreed after an alternative proposal not to buy either plot was put forward.

Each purchase is subject to legal due diligence and checks on title, confirmation of the land's planning status and any covenants or easements, a valuation showing value for money, and agreement of final terms including price and timescales. The Director of Neighbourhood Services and Communities, in consultation with the chair of the Strategy and Resources Committee, can agree the final price. The valuation and negotiation details were considered in private and have not been published.
points: Full council decision on Thursday 22 October 2026
Two plots at Langford, sold at auction in 2025
Price can be up to 10% above an independent valuation, raised from 5% in the report

councilwatch.headline: New rules for licensed pet and animal businesses across Basildon borough adopted until 2031
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Council has formally adopted an Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter for 2026 to 2031, replacing its old Animal Welfare Charter after a public consultation.
body: Basildon Council's Licensing Committee formally adopted a new Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter for 2026 to 2031 on Monday 2 November 2026. The policy covers how the council licenses, inspects and takes enforcement action against licensed animal activities across all wards of the borough, which includes Basildon, Billericay and Wickford.

The report says the new policy replaces the council's previous Animal Welfare Charter and is intended to promote high standards of animal welfare and a consistent, transparent and proportionate approach to licensing. After a public consultation, the Licensing Committee backed amendments on 17 September 2026, including stronger provisions on intelligence sharing and recognition of the role played by reputable animal rescue and rehoming centres. The council's Cabinet endorsed the policy on 15 October 2026 and referred it back for final adoption.

The report says licence fees depend on the length of licence granted, which in turn depends on the risk rating of the premises, with lower risk premises generally granted longer licences. The adopted policy and charter are published with the committee papers, with the consultation amendments highlighted.

councilwatch.headline: Developer appeals over lack of decision on 910 green belt homes at Billericay's Foots Farm
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee was asked to say how it would have decided the Great Burstead scheme, after an appeal was lodged because no decision had been made. Officers backed the plan, which offers more than £20 million in contributions.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee considered an outline application for up to 910 homes on land at Foots Farm, Southend Road, Great Burstead, near Billericay, on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Because the applicant had already lodged an appeal on the grounds of non-determination, councillors were asked to indicate the decision they would have made had the application stayed with the council. Officers recommended that outline planning permission would have been granted.

The report says the 56.89 hectare site is farmland in the Metropolitan Green Belt and that the scheme counts as inappropriate development, but officers concluded its benefits significantly outweigh the harm. Half the homes would be affordable, with eight Gypsy and Traveller pitches, a community hub and 3.44 hectares safeguarded for a nursery and three-form entry primary school. The Section 106 package of more than £20 million covers education, healthcare, bus services, play and sports, and employment and skills, and the site forms part of the South East Billericay allocation in the emerging Basildon Local Plan.

Three residents and the chair of the parish council spoke against the plan, citing the loss of Green Belt and farmland, traffic on Coxes Farm Road and Bell Hill, and pressure on schools, GP services, water supply and drainage. Councillors also complained that a technical briefing had been arranged without consulting the committee's chair and vice-chair and without Essex County Council Highways, and it was agreed to seek Highways representation at future meetings. The application will now be settled through the appeal.
points: Up to 910 homes, 50% affordable, on 56.89 hectares of Green Belt
Section 106 contributions in excess of £20 million
3.44 hectares safeguarded for a nursery and primary school
Appeal lodged on the grounds of non-determination

councilwatch.headline: Basildon councillors confirm refusal of 175 green belt homes at Little Burstead
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee agreed the formal grounds for turning down homes west of Tye Common Road, near Billericay, going against officers' advice to approve.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee agreed on Tuesday 3 November 2026 the formal reason for refusing outline permission for up to 175 homes on land west of Tye Common Road, Little Burstead, near Billericay. Councillors had resolved to refuse the scheme at their meeting on Wednesday 7 October 2026, and the wording was brought back for agreement. The vote was 5 in favour, none against and 2 abstentions, with two councillors who missed the earlier meeting taking no part.

The agreed reason says the site makes a strong contribution to the Green Belt's purpose of checking urban sprawl, so it does not count as grey belt, and the homes would cause substantial harm to the openness of the Green Belt. The committee was not satisfied that the benefits clearly outweighed that harm. Officers had recommended approval, pointing to 50% affordable housing, public open space, biodiversity gains and financial contributions.
The report notes that the risks of planning decisions relate to appeals, cost awards and judicial review. The applicant can appeal against the refusal to the Planning Inspectorate.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring councillors to vote on sending Local Plan for 1,069 homes a year to a government inspector
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council's local plan committee meets on 17 November to decide whether to recommend submitting the plan, with Kirby Cross, Brightlingsea, Bradfield and Frinton sites drawing most objections.
body: Tendring District Council's Planning Policy and Local Plan Committee will meet on Tuesday 17 November 2026 to hear the results of the final public consultation on the district's new Local Plan, held in September and October 2026. Councillors are asked to recommend to Full Council that the plan be submitted to the Secretary of State for independent examination by a planning inspector. Officers say they remain of the view that the plan is legally compliant and sound.

The report says government targets require Tendring to plan for 1,069 homes a year, nearly double the figure in its previous plan. The council aims to submit before the end of 2026, even though the government has extended the cut-off to the end of March 2027, to avoid restarting under a new system. Fewer people responded than at the previous stage, when 628 respondents made about 2,200 comments, mainly because the council dropped two of the most opposed sites, at Brightlingsea and Walton.

The most opposed remaining site is the planned 450 homes north of Thorpe Road, Kirby Cross, with about 45 objections, and the report notes Taylor Wimpey has been consulting on up to 500 homes there, with an application possible in December. A 2,600-name petition, around 500 of them from the Manningtree, Lawford and Mistley area, backed keeping Lawford Tye as protected open space, and 12 of Tendring's 27 town and parish councils responded. The final decision to submit rests with Full Council, and the inspector may require changes before the plan can be adopted.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon scraps area planning committees and councillor call-in as new national rules take effect
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council now has one 13-member Planning Committee, with most applications decided by officers under a new national scheme of delegation.
body: Maldon District Council agreed on Thursday 22 October 2026 to set up a single Planning Committee of 13 members from Saturday 31 October 2026. It abolished the North Western, Central and South Eastern Area Planning Committees and the District Planning Committee on the same date. Councillors were told the change was required by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026, which came into force on 31 October.

Under the new National Scheme of Delegation, routine and minor applications go to officers, and larger or more sensitive ones are also delegated unless they pass a threshold known as the Gateway Test. There is no longer a process for councillors to call in applications. Councillor W Stamp said she did not consider the changes democratic and asked for her vote against to be recorded.

The new committee is due to meet every three weeks at 7pm, mostly on Wednesdays, with meetings cancelled when there is no business. A separate report to the same meeting proposed a revised public speaking protocol that would let ward councillors who do not sit on the committee speak on applications in their wards, raise speaking time from two to three minutes, and allow electronic voting.
points: One 13-member Planning Committee from 31 October 2026
Four previous planning committees abolished
No councillor call-in under the national scheme
Meetings every three weeks at 7pm when there is business

councilwatch.headline: Maldon's share of the halted Mid Essex unitary council set-up costs put at about £26,000
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council councillors have asked for a full breakdown, including officer time, of spending on the Mid Essex council plan before the government paused the Essex shake-up.
body: Maldon District Council received a report from its Chief Executive on Thursday 22 October 2026 setting out what it spent preparing for a Mid Essex unitary council before the government paused local government reorganisation. Councillors agreed to ask for a full breakdown of the costs, including officer time, and details of how the Mid Essex Director was appointed.

The report says the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government withdrew the five-unitary model for Essex on 7 September 2026 and paused reorganisation for review. Costs between the choice of that model and the pause are estimated at £78,000, with Maldon expected to pay a third, about £26,000, for IT, a councillor engagement event, staff support and specialist project management. No posts were recruited specifically for the work, and earlier Freedom of Information requests about the costs were refused because the figures were due to be published.

The final figure is due to be confirmed by the Mid Essex Programme Board in November, and the council is still waiting to hear whether there are Essex-wide costs to share. Councillors were also told that Essex County Council has consented to a Greater Essex mayoral strategic authority with Southend-on-Sea City Council and Thurrock Council, though all three must agree, and that the first mayoral election is now planned for May 2028.

councilwatch.headline: Government direction pushes Southend's draft local plan towards a six-week public consultation
councilwatch.summary: The new plan would set the rules for where homes go and how the council handles applications for shared houses, affordable housing and hot food takeaways.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's cabinet held an extraordinary meeting on 5 November 2026 to consider the final draft of the city's new Local Plan. A report from the Executive Director (Environment and Place) sought agreement to comply with a government direction by publishing the Regulation 19 Proposed Submission version of the plan for a consultation lasting at least six weeks. At this stage residents and others can comment on whether the plan is sound and legally compliant.

The minutes say national policy requires every council to keep an up-to-date local plan, which allocates sites for development and sets the policies used to decide planning applications. Councillors were told the existing Development Plan is out of date and no longer reflects major social, environmental and economic changes. The reasons recorded for the decision warn that without a plan development would not stop, but would be more likely to come forward in an uncoordinated and speculative way, with less supporting infrastructure and fewer protections for existing residents.

The papers say new criteria-based policies would give the council a more robust, evidenced approach to applications including Houses in Multiple Occupation, affordable housing and hot food takeaways. The meeting papers include the draft plan, a policies map, a report on the earlier Regulation 18 consultation, a sustainability appraisal and an updated Local Development Scheme setting out the timetable. Three questions from councillors were answered at the meeting and published with the minutes.

Report sought agreement to publish the Regulation 19 draft plan under a government direction

councilwatch.summary: KPMG told councillors its audit of the 2025/26 accounts is on track, with work still under way on the value of council homes.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's external auditor, KPMG, reported on its audit of the council's accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 at the Audit and Governance Committee on 19 October 2026. KPMG said the work was progressing well and remained on track to be completed ahead of the statutory deadline. The committee noted the report.

Councillors were told of a £1.7 million unadjusted audit difference relating to pension liabilities, along with several control findings on property valuations and declarations of related party interests. Some risks identified at the planning stage had been removed after testing, but work was continuing on the valuation of council dwellings and on journal testing. Members asked about a fall in the value of council homes, proposed changes to the audit fee and how related party declarations are handled.

KPMG confirmed that officers had continued to support the audit and said there were no concerns about meeting the January 2027 deadline. At the same meeting the committee heard that a national financial resilience index placed Southend 30th of 62 comparable unitary councils, which officers described as a broadly average position.

councilwatch.summary: Electrical safety checks on council homes are now close to complete, but councillors heard that repairs remain the weak spot in Southend's response to the social housing regulator.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Audit and Governance Committee received an update on 19 October 2026 on the council's progress in responding to a judgement by the Regulator of Social Housing. The report, from the Executive Director for Environment and Place, also covered the council's dealings with the Housing Ombudsman and the Building Safety Regulator.

The Head of Housing told the committee that monthly meetings with the regulator were continuing and that significant progress had been made on the council's Provider Improvement Plan. The council has reached 100% coverage of electrical safety checks in communal areas and 99% in homes, and the minutes say the regulator now regards electrical safety as business as usual. Repairs remain an area of focus, and a targeted improvement plan has been agreed with the council's repairs contractor to cut work in progress and bring performance up to industry norms by Christmas 2026.

Councillors were told the Housing Ombudsman's investigation has concluded, with the council due to submit a learning statement as the final stage. Officers said this was the first inspection under the new consumer regulation framework and that the council knew of areas needing improvement before the inspections took place. The committee asked for a further update on repairs performance.

body: Thurrock Council's Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 22 October 2026 that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care are now completed within the statutory 20-day timescale. The figure compares with 36% previously, according to the minutes of the meeting.

Officers put the improvement down to closer joint working with Children's Services, more paediatric capacity and better oversight. They said late assessments were mainly caused by changes of placement, hospital admissions, missed appointments and occasional staff absence, and that only one delayed assessment in the reporting period was down to a lack of capacity.

The service is moving to a model led by specialist nurses working with paediatricians, and officers said a formal review in December 2026 will look at the views of children and families, the quality of assessments and timeliness. Councillors questioned whether enough paediatric capacity would remain, and officers said the aim was to use existing paediatric resources more effectively. The committee noted the update.

councilwatch.summary: A motion to full council called for the district's maximum fixed penalty for fly-tipping to rise fivefold now that the law allows it.
body: A motion put to Epping Forest District Council's full council meeting on 22 October 2026 asked councillors to support, in principle, raising the council's maximum fixed penalty notice for fly-tipping from £1,000 to £5,000. It was proposed by Councillor K Rizvi and seconded by Councillor C McCann. The published papers do not yet record the outcome.

The motion says the council can currently issue fines of up to £1,000 for fly-tipping, but recent changes to the law now allow councils to set a maximum of £5,000. It argues that people who deliberately dump waste should face a penalty reflecting the damage to the environment and the costs borne by residents.

If backed, the motion asks the Cabinet Member for Environment and Regulatory Services to work with the council's environmental enforcement team to bring in the higher fine as soon as practicable, subject to legal and constitutional requirements. It also calls for clear public communication and continued enforcement, and encourages residents to keep reporting fly-tipping with photographs, CCTV or dashcam footage where they have it.

body: Tendring District Council's cabinet will be asked on 13 November 2026 to adopt updated Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans for St Osyth and for Manningtree and Mistley. The report from the Portfolio Holder for Housing and Planning recommends adoption, including revised conservation area boundaries where applicable.

The report says both documents were shaped by public consultations held between 2022 and 2026, and that responses led to changes, including to some boundaries. Once adopted, the appraisals would become material planning considerations, meaning they would carry weight when planning applications in those areas are decided. They are the last two in a programme to review all 20 of the district's conservation areas, a priority of the Tendring Heritage Strategy, which includes five areas on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.

The report says that without adoption the council could not give weight to the updated appraisals in planning decisions, and its ability to conserve the district's historic environment would be reduced. The documents are also intended to inform the council's emerging Local Plan.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring budgets for life beyond 2028 as the government pauses the council shake-up
councilwatch.summary: With Whitehall reviewing its plan to replace Essex's councils, Tendring's cabinet has agreed to plan four years ahead, and backed money for toilets, playgrounds and housing staff.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet has agreed to refresh the council's financial forecast over four years, to allow for the possibility that the council still exists after April 2028. That date had been the proposed start for a new unitary council under the government's original timetable for Greater Essex, but on 7 September 2026 the government announced it would pause and review its local government reorganisation programme.

The report to cabinet on 23 October said the pause had brought a significant level of uncertainty for the councils affected, though Tendring's two-year financial plan still left it in a positive position. If reorganisation goes ahead, even later than planned, the forecast can be switched back to the council's earlier approach of preparing for a handover to the new authority.

Cabinet also approved changes to this year's budget, including £540,000 for housing capacity and restructuring, £100,000 to invest in public toilets and £400,000 for project delivery capacity, and accepted £270,000 from the government's Playground Fund. The report said the general fund was £3.669m underspent against its profiled budget at the end of July, largely because of the timing of spending.
points: Forecast to be refreshed over four years in case the council continues beyond April 2028
Government paused its reorganisation programme on 7 September 2026
£270,000 Playground Fund grant accepted and £100,000 set aside for public toilets
General fund £3.669m underspent at the end of July, mostly down to timing

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock's special needs funding gap keeps growing as Treetops School plans 110 more places
councilwatch.summary: Children's services are on course to underspend by about £0.5m, but the grant that pays for special educational needs is heading deeper into deficit, councillors heard.
body: Thurrock Council's children's services are forecast to underspend by about £0.5 million this year, councillors on the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee heard on 22 October. Officers said the underspend came largely from making the most of grants and from staff vacancies, which offset rising demand, and that all planned savings had been achieved.

The committee was also told about pressure on the high needs block of the Dedicated Schools Grant, which pays for special educational needs provision. Officers said forecasts showed a growing deficit despite investment in local specialist places, and that national funding arrangements and reform proposals would be critical to its long-term sustainability, with government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit.

Officers confirmed that 110 additional places were planned at Treetops School through a phased expansion, which would add local specialist capacity and reduce reliance on placements outside the borough. They said feedback from the Department for Education on the council's submission had been positive, focusing on extra detail and measurable outcomes rather than finances. The committee noted the forecast.
points: Children's services forecast to underspend by about £0.5m
High needs deficit growing despite investment in local places
110 more places planned at Treetops School in a phased expansion
Government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock picked as one of seven national pilots helping children stay with their wider family
councilwatch.summary: The Kinship Zones pilot will give practical, emotional and financial support to relatives raising children, as Thurrock reshapes its children's social care.
body: Thurrock has been selected as one of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities, councillors heard at the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 22 October. The pilot aims to help children stay safely within their wider family networks, with practical, emotional and financial support for kinship carers and fewer care proceedings.

It is part of the council's Families First Partnership programme, which aims to step in earlier and support whole families. Officers said ten Family Help Teams had been set up and a single assessment and planning framework introduced, and that work was under way on a Multi-Agency Child Protection Team bringing together professionals from partner organisations.

The committee also heard that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care were now completed within the statutory 20 days, up from 36% previously. Officers credited closer joint working, more paediatric capacity and better oversight, and said a formal review of the new nurse-led and paediatrician model would take place in December 2026.
points: One of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities
Ten Family Help Teams now in place
75% of health checks for children entering care now on time, up from 36%
Review of the new health assessment model due in December

councilwatch.headline: Southend's fraud investigators have brought in more than £800,000 for the council this year
councilwatch.summary: School admissions fraud and Blue Badge misuse were among the areas councillors raised as the council's counter fraud team reported on its work.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Counter Fraud and Investigation Team has generated benefits of more than £800,000 for the council so far this financial year, the Audit and Governance Committee heard on 19 October.

Councillors discussed recent work on school admissions fraud. Officers said referrals came from school admissions officers, members of the public and the team's own proactive investigations, and that growing public awareness had led to more referrals. Members also asked about Blue Badge enforcement and future investigation exercises.

The committee heard that a new fraud investigator had been recruited and that a number of investigations involving council employees were continuing. Officers said details could not be disclosed for confidentiality reasons, but that criminal prosecutions continued to be pursued where appropriate. The committee noted the report.
points: Benefits of more than £800,000 so far this financial year
More school admissions fraud referrals as awareness grows
Blue Badge enforcement raised by councillors
New fraud investigator recruited
